description: Researching companies, understanding different interview processes, and building a concrete preparation plan for a specific target.

lessons.title: Researching companies before you apply
objectives: Research a company's product, engineering culture, and recent context before interviewing
Explain how product familiarity changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect product familiarity with engineering blog signals and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Real company research goes beyond the homepage: understand the actual product (use it if possible), recent news (funding, layoffs, launches — these shape interview mood and questions), engineering blog posts (reveal real technical priorities and stack), and what the interview process is known to look like (from company engineering blogs.
examples:
# minimum useful research before any interview:
# 1. use the actual product if you can
# 2. read their engineering blog's most recent 2-3 posts
# 3. check recent news (funding, layoffs, major launches)
# 4. note what tech stack/keywords keep appearing
commonMistakes: Walking into an interview only knowing the company's one-line pitch — interviewers routinely notice, and reward, genuine familiarity with what they actually build.
lessons.careerRelevance: Company research directly shapes which resume bullets and stories you lead with — untailored preparation reads as generic to an interviewer.
lessons.explain: Real company research goes beyond the homepage: understand the actual product (use it if possible), recent news (funding, layoffs, launches — these shape interview mood and questions), engineering blog posts (reveal real technical priorities and stack), and what the interview process is known to look like (from company engineering blogs.

lessons.title: Reading job descriptions to reverse-engineer what's tested
objectives: Extract the actual evaluation criteria hidden inside a job posting
Explain how requirement-to-topic mapping changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect requirement-to-topic mapping with behavioral signal extraction and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A job description is a compressed signal of what will actually be evaluated: required skills map to technical screening topics, listed responsibilities hint at what real work (and likely behavioral questions) to expect, and repeated terms usually indicate genuine priorities, not filler.
examples:
# JD says: 'Design and maintain RESTful APIs, work with PostgreSQL, collaborate in an agile team'
# -> expect: API design questions, some SQL/database questions,
# and a behavioral question about team collaboration
concepts: signals extracted from the job description
commonMistakes: Skimming a job description once and moving on — a careful second pass, listing every implied evaluation area, produces a genuinely useful personal prep checklist.
lessons.careerRelevance: This reverse-engineering skill directly connects to the Resume Preparation track's tailoring lesson — the same JD read informs both documents.
lessons.explain: A job description is a compressed signal of what will actually be evaluated: required skills map to technical screening topics, listed responsibilities hint at what real work (and likely behavioral questions) to expect, and repeated terms usually indicate genuine priorities, not filler.
lessons.example:
# JD says: 'Design and maintain RESTful APIs, work with PostgreSQL, collaborate in an agile team'
# -> expect: API design questions, some SQL/database questions,
# and a behavioral question about team collaboration

lessons.title: Startup interviews: what's different
objectives: Contrast startup interview processes and expectations against larger companies
Explain how speed & informality changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect speed & informality with versatility over specialization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Startup interviews are often faster (fewer rounds, quicker decisions), more likely to test broad, hands-on versatility over deep specialization, and weigh cultural/mission fit heavily since small teams feel every hire's impact directly.
examples:
# startup interview signals to expect:
# - fewer, faster rounds than a large company
# - more 'how would you build/approach this' open discussion
# - genuine interest in why THIS company/mission, not just 'why tech'
commonMistakes: Preparing for a startup exactly like a big-company interview loop — over-rehearsed, rigid answers can read as a poor culture fit for a team valuing scrappiness and directness.
lessons.careerRelevance: Startup interview dynamics are genuinely different enough that generic 'FAANG prep' alone under-prepares a candidate for them.
lessons.explain: Startup interviews are often faster (fewer rounds, quicker decisions), more likely to test broad, hands-on versatility over deep specialization, and weigh cultural/mission fit heavily since small teams feel every hire's impact directly.

lessons.title: The FAANG-style interview process
objectives: Describe the typical structure of a large tech company's interview process
Explain how structured, multi-round process changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect structured, multi-round process with standardized rubrics and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Large tech companies (and companies that model their process similarly, sometimes called FAANG-style) typically run: an initial recruiter screen, one or more technical phone/video screens (often a live coding platform), an onsite or virtual loop with multiple rounds (coding, system design for more senior roles, behavioral).
examples:
# typical loop shape:
# recruiter screen -> 1-2 technical phone screens -> onsite loop
# (coding x2, system design, behavioral) -> hiring committee decision
# -- each round is often scored independently against a rubric, not just a gut call
commonMistakes: Assuming one strong round can compensate for a weak one, or that the interviewer alone makes the final call — many large companies use committee review across ALL round feedback, not a.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this structure specifically helps set realistic expectations and reduces anxiety about any single round feeling decisive.
lessons.explain: Large tech companies (and companies that model their process similarly, sometimes called FAANG-style) typically run: an initial recruiter screen, one or more technical phone/video screens (often a live coding platform), an onsite or virtual loop with multiple rounds (coding, system design for more senior roles, behavioral).

lessons.title: Enterprise company interviews: what's different
objectives: Contrast large, established enterprise interviews against startup and FAANG-style processes
Explain how process & stakeholder skills changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect process & stakeholder skills with domain relevance and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Established, non-tech-native enterprises (banks, traditional large corporations building internal software) often weigh process discipline, communication, and stakeholder-management skills more heavily alongside coding ability, reflecting how the actual job operates.
examples:
# enterprise interview signals to expect:
# - real interest in how you handle process, documentation, and stakeholders
# - domain knowledge (finance, healthcare, etc.) can matter as much as raw coding skill
# - often slower-moving processes than a startup or tech-native company
commonMistakes: Preparing only pure algorithmic coding prep for a role where the actual day-to-day and interview both weight process/communication heavily — research the SPECIFIC company's actual emphasis.
lessons.careerRelevance: Recognizing this distinction avoids both over- and under-preparing for a specific employer's real evaluation criteria.
lessons.explain: Established, non-tech-native enterprises (banks, traditional large corporations building internal software) often weigh process discipline, communication, and stakeholder-management skills more heavily alongside coding ability, reflecting how the actual job operates.

lessons.title: Preparing projects that match the role
objectives: Select and prepare to discuss projects that map directly to a target role
Explain how role-relevant project selection changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect role-relevant project selection with structured project narratives and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Given limited interview time, the projects you bring up should map directly to what the target role and company actually need — a role emphasizing backend APIs is better served by discussing your Backend Development track projects in depth than a frontend side project, even if the latter is more polished.
examples:
# structure for discussing a project in an interview:
# 1. the problem/goal in one sentence
# 2. your specific role/contribution (not just 'the team')
# 3. one interesting technical decision or trade-off you made
# 4. the outcome, ideally with some concrete measure
commonMistakes: Discussing a group project purely in terms of 'we did X' with no clarity on your own specific contribution — interviewers need to isolate YOUR actual skill and judgment from the team's.
lessons.careerRelevance: Well-prepared, role-relevant project stories are often what most directly differentiates similarly-skilled candidates in an interview.
lessons.explain: Given limited interview time, the projects you bring up should map directly to what the target role and company actually need — a role emphasizing backend APIs is better served by discussing your Backend Development track projects in depth than a frontend side project, even if the latter is more polished.
lessons.example:

lessons.title: Coding assessment strategies
objectives: Apply a systematic strategy for timed online coding assessments
Explain how assessment triage changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect assessment triage with brute-force-first under time pressure and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Timed coding assessments (OAs) reward strategy alongside raw ability: read ALL problems first and triage by difficulty/point value before diving in, don't get stuck on one problem burning all your remaining time, write and test the brute-force solution first if you're unsure of the optimal approach (partial credit usually beats no submission).
examples:
# OA time-management strategy:
# 1. skim ALL problems first, note relative difficulty/points
# 2. start with the one you're most confident about
# 3. get a working brute-force submission before attempting to optimize
# 4. reserve the last 10-15% of time for edge-case review across all problems
commonMistakes: Spending 70% of the available time perfecting the first problem and running out of time for the rest — triage and partial-credit strategy usually beats depth-first perfectionism on one.
lessons.careerRelevance: This strategic, time-aware approach is directly what separates candidates of similar raw skill in timed assessment outcomes.
lessons.explain: Timed coding assessments (OAs) reward strategy alongside raw ability: read ALL problems first and triage by difficulty/point value before diving in, don't get stuck on one problem burning all your remaining time, write and test the brute-force solution first if you're unsure of the optimal approach (partial credit usually beats no submission).

lessons.title: Building your 30-day interview preparation plan
objectives: Assemble a concrete, week-by-week preparation plan for a target company/role
Explain how structured multi-week planning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect structured multi-week planning with matching practice to job-description signals and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pulling together every track covered so far into one concrete plan: week 1 focuses on company/role research and resume tailoring (Resume Preparation track), weeks 2-3 focus on technical practice matched to what the job description signals (DSA, system design, or domain-specific practice as relevant).
examples:
# a realistic 30-day skeleton:
# Week 1: company research + resume/LinkedIn tailoring + JD analysis
# Week 2-3: targeted technical practice (DSA/system design/domain-specific, per the JD)
# Week 4: mock interviews, behavioral story rehearsal, final portfolio/resume check
concepts: mock-interview cadence in the final stretch
commonMistakes: Preparing with no explicit plan or timeline, so effort ends up unevenly spread — a concrete week-by-week plan makes sure resume, technical practice, and mock interviews all actually happen.
lessons.careerRelevance: This synthesis lesson is the direct, practical payoff of every other lesson across the Resume, Interview, and Company Preparation tracks.

lessons.title: Evaluating salary, offers & onboarding
objectives: Evaluate a job offer holistically and prepare for onboarding
Explain how total compensation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect total compensation with offer evaluation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A job offer is more than a base salary number: total compensation includes equity, bonus, benefits, and non-monetary factors like growth trajectory and team fit. Once accepted, onboarding is its own skill -- asking good questions early, understanding team norms, and setting a realistic ramp-up expectation for yourself in the first 90 days.
examples:
# comparing two offers fairly means looking at:
# base + bonus + equity (realistically valued) + benefits + growth trajectory
# not just comparing the base salary number alone
commonMistakes: Comparing job offers by base salary alone, ignoring equity, bonus structure, benefits, and growth trajectory differences.
lessons.careerRelevance: Evaluating offers holistically, and onboarding well, directly affects both your finances and how your first months at a new job go.

lessons.title: Professional communication & career planning
objectives: Communicate professionally and plan your career deliberately
Explain how professional communication changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect professional communication with career planning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Professional communication (clear status updates, asking for help appropriately, giving and receiving feedback) compounds over a career far more than any single technical skill.
examples:
# a good status update: what's done, what's blocked, what's needed --
# not just 'still working on it'
# career planning: revisit your goals every 6-12 months, not never
commonMistakes: Never deliberately revisiting career goals, and only reacting to whatever task or opportunity happens to appear next.
lessons.careerRelevance: Professional communication and deliberate career planning are durable skills that compound across an entire career, not just one job.

quiz.q: Reading a job description carefully mainly helps you:
options: guess the salary
reverse-engineer likely technical and behavioral evaluation topics
skip the interview
write better code automatically

quiz.q: Startup interviews compared to FAANG-style companies are generally:
options: identical in every way
often faster, less standardized, and weigh fit/versatility more heavily
always harder technically
never technical at all

quiz.q: In a FAANG-style process, hiring decisions are typically made by:
options: a single interviewer's gut feeling
a committee reviewing standardized feedback across rounds
the recruiter alone
random selection

quiz.q: When discussing a group project in an interview, it's most important to:
options: only describe what 'the team' did
clearly isolate your own specific contribution and decisions
avoid mentioning teammates entirely
focus only on the tech stack used

quiz.q: A good OA time-management strategy is to:
options: perfect the first problem before looking at the others
triage all problems first, then work strategically with time reserved for review
skip reading the problems and start coding immediately
always solve problems in the order given

quiz.q: Why research a company's engineering blog before an interview?
options: engineering blogs are irrelevant to interview prep
it reveals real technical priorities, tools, and challenges the company actually cares about, informing what to prepare for
engineering blogs are only for marketing purposes
this research only matters after receiving an offer

quiz.q: Why does recent company context (news, product launches) matter for interview prep?
options: recent context has no bearing on interviews
it signals genuine interest and can inform thoughtful questions during the interview
recent news should never be mentioned in interviews
only historical company information matters

quiz.q: What does reverse-engineering a job description mean?
options: ignoring the job description entirely
inferring likely interview topics and evaluation criteria from the specific skills and requirements listed
rewriting the job description yourself
applying to a different role instead

quiz.q: Why extract 'priority terms' from a job description?
options: priority terms have no practical use
terms mentioned prominently or repeatedly often reflect what the role/interview will emphasize most
priority terms are randomly distributed with no signal
only the job title matters, not the description details

quiz.q: What typically characterizes startup interviews compared to larger companies?
options: startups always have longer, more formal processes
greater speed and informality, often valuing versatility over narrow specialization
startups never conduct technical interviews
startup interviews are always easier

quiz.q: Why might startups weight mission/fit more heavily in interviews?
options: mission and fit are irrelevant at startups
smaller teams with less structure often rely more on shared motivation and adaptability to succeed
startups never consider cultural fit
this only applies to non-technical roles

quiz.q: What typically characterizes a FAANG-style interview process?
options: a single informal conversation
a structured, multi-round process often using standardized rubrics and committee-based decisions
no technical evaluation at all
a process identical to every startup's approach

quiz.q: Why do FAANG-style companies often use standardized rubrics?
options: rubrics are unnecessary bureaucracy
they aim for more consistent, comparable evaluation across many candidates and interviewers
rubrics guarantee identical interview questions for everyone
rubrics eliminate the need for any interviewer judgment

quiz.q: What tends to differ in enterprise company interviews compared to startups?
options: enterprise interviews are always shorter
enterprise loops often move slower and weight stakeholder/process skills and domain relevance more heavily
enterprise companies never conduct technical interviews
there's no meaningful difference between the two

quiz.q: Why select projects that match the specific role you're applying for?
options: project selection has no bearing on interview outcomes
demonstrating directly relevant experience makes your fit for the specific role clearer and more convincing
you should always present your most complex project regardless of relevance
interviewers never ask about past projects

quiz.q: What does 'specific contribution framing' mean when discussing a team project?
options: describing the team's work without your individual role
clearly articulating YOUR specific contributions within a team effort, not just the team's overall outcome
never mentioning teamwork at all
claiming full credit for all team outcomes

quiz.q: Why triage problems during a timed coding assessment?
options: triage wastes valuable time
quickly assessing which problems are feasible within the time limit helps prioritize effort toward what's achievable
all problems should always be attempted in the given order
triage is only relevant for open-ended assessments

quiz.q: Why do an edge-case review pass before submitting a coding assessment?
options: edge cases are rarely tested in assessments
many automated graders specifically test boundary conditions, and a final review pass can catch issues before submission
review passes are unnecessary if the main logic works
edge cases matter only in real production code, never assessments

quiz.q: Why build a structured, multi-week interview preparation plan rather than cramming?
options: cramming is always equally effective
spaced, structured practice over weeks builds more durable skill and confidence than last-minute cramming
preparation plans have no real effect on interview performance
a single day of preparation is always sufficient

quiz.q: Why match practice problems to signals extracted from the job description?
options: practice should always be generic and unrelated to the specific role
targeting practice toward what the role/company actually emphasizes makes preparation time more efficient
job descriptions never provide useful preparation signals
practice matching only matters for junior roles

quiz.q: Why increase mock-interview frequency in the final stretch before a real interview?
options: mock interviews are only useful early in preparation
concentrated realistic practice close to the actual interview helps sharpen readiness and reduce nerves
mock interviews should be spread evenly with no change in frequency
mock interviews become less useful the more you do them

quiz.q: Why evaluate a job offer's total compensation rather than base salary alone?
options: base salary is the only component that matters
equity, bonus, and benefits can represent significant additional value beyond the base salary number
total compensation is a meaningless concept
non-salary components are never negotiable or relevant

quiz.q: Why is onboarding considered its own skill, not just 'starting a job'?
options: onboarding requires no particular effort or approach
asking good questions early and setting realistic ramp-up expectations meaningfully affects how well the first months go
onboarding is identical at every company with no adaptation needed
onboarding only matters for senior hires

quiz.q: Why should career planning be revisited periodically rather than never?
options: career goals never change once set
skills, market conditions, and personal priorities evolve, so periodic reflection keeps your trajectory intentional rather than purely reactive
career planning is only relevant when actively job-hunting
revisiting career goals is a sign of indecision

quiz.q: What distinguishes a good status update from a vague one?
options: vague updates are equally useful
a good status update specifies what's done, what's blocked, and what's needed, rather than a non-specific 'still working on it'
status updates should never mention blockers
specificity in updates is unnecessary overhead

quiz.q: Why does professional communication compound in value over a career?
options: communication skills have no lasting career impact
clear, professional communication affects how you're perceived and collaborated with across every future role and interaction, not just one job
only technical skill matters for career growth
communication skills can't be improved through practice

quiz.q: Why prepare differently for a startup interview versus an enterprise interview?
options: all interview processes are functionally identical
different company types weight speed, structure, specialization, and process differently, so preparation should reflect the actual context
startups and enterprises always evaluate identical criteria
only technical skills differ between these company types

quiz.q: Why does understanding a company's product matter before interviewing there?
options: product knowledge is irrelevant to most technical interviews
genuine product familiarity often informs better questions and demonstrates real interest during the interview
only sales roles require product knowledge
product research should happen only after receiving an offer

quiz.q: What is a reasonable approach to comparing two job offers with different equity structures?
options: only compare the base salary figures
realistically value the equity (considering vesting, company stage, and liquidity) alongside base, bonus, and benefits
ignore equity entirely since it's never guaranteed
always choose whichever offer has more equity regardless of other factors

quiz.q: Why might requirement-to-topic mapping from a job description be a useful preparation technique?
options: job descriptions provide no useful preparation signal
translating each listed requirement into a likely interview topic focuses preparation on what's actually likely to be tested
this technique only works for non-technical roles
requirements should be ignored in favor of generic preparation
